title: Smallest Order by Swapping Close Values
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers and a number limit. In one move you may swap any two entries nums[i] and nums[j] whose values differ by at most limit, that is |nums[i] − nums[j]| ≤ limit. You can make as many moves as you like.

Return the lexicographically smallest array you can reach: compare arrays position by position, and the first position where they differ decides.

examples.why: 4 and 10 differ by 6, but both can swap with 7, so 4, 7 and 10 can end up in any order in their slots (0, 1, 3). 18 and 20 share slots 2 and 4.
No chain of close values links 2 to 6 or 7, so the 2 can never reach the front. The best is to sort each group within its own slots.
Every pair is close enough, so the whole array can be sorted.

hints: Swaps chain: if a can swap with b and b with c, then a, b and c can be arranged in any order among their positions. Which values end up in the same group?
Sort the values. Two values that are neighbours in sorted order and differ by at most limit are in the same group; a bigger gap splits the groups, since nothing can bridge it.
For each group, sort its positions and its values, then put the smallest value in the smallest position, and so on.

explain.intuition:
Think of values as nodes and connect two values when they are close enough to swap. Inside a connected group, repeated swaps can produce any arrangement of the group's values over the group's positions. Between groups nothing ever moves. So the best result is: within each group, put its smallest value in its earliest position, the next smallest in the next position, and so on.

Finding the groups does not need a graph. Sort the values: a group is a run in sorted order where each step to the next value is at most limit. If the gap between two sorted neighbours is bigger than limit, every value below the gap is too far from every value above it.
steps: Make the list of indexes 0..n−1 sorted by nums[index].
Walk it and cut a new group whenever the next value exceeds the previous one by more than limit.
For each group: its values are already in sorted order; sort its indexes ascending.
Write the i-th smallest value of the group into the i-th smallest index of the group.
pitfalls: Comparing each value only with the group's first value. Groups grow by chaining: 4 and 10 are in one group through 7.
Sorting each group's values but leaving them at their old positions in sorted-value order. The positions must be sorted separately.
Swapping greedily from the left with the nearest close value. A value can only reach the front through a chain, which a local scan does not see.

solutions.title: Union every close pair, then sort each group
solutions.idea: Join every pair of positions whose values are within limit with union-find, then sort values and positions inside each component.

solutions.title: Sort once, cut at big gaps
solutions.idea: In sorted order, groups are maximal runs whose consecutive gaps are at most limit. Deal each run's values into its sorted positions.

followups: Each swap now costs 1. What is the fewest swaps needed to reach the smallest array?
Instead of a value rule, you get an explicit list of index pairs that may be swapped. How do you find the groups then?
lcTitle: Make Lexicographically Smallest Array by Swapping Elements
